summary: The Katherine Johnson Space Heritage operates as an innovative hybrid ecosystem that connects urban spaces with digital technology to democratize space exploration. By rescuing the history of abandoned and discarded space hardware scattered across the Moon, Mars, and deep space, the project addresses the lack of engagement among young audiences with complex technical archives. On the physical side, it features the installation of open-air informational totems in plazas, parks, and schools—equipped with bilingual plaques, full-scale tactile replicas, and QR codes that, when scanned, instantly reveal the story of each space artifact and transform silent monuments into accessible educational narratives. On the digital side, the platform runs through a Progressive Web App (PWA) and Augmented Reality (AR) application. Using official NASA data (such as JPL Horizons), the app functions as a pocket cosmic compass: users point their smartphones at the sky to track active missions or view the last recorded coordinates of probes, rovers, and landers that have lost contact with the agency, complemented by first-person logbooks and a gamified space passport.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

The Katherine Johnson Space Heritage operates as an innovative hybrid ecosystem that connects urban spaces with digital technology to democratize space exploration. On the physical side, the project features the installation of open-air informational totems in plazas, parks, and schools, equipped with bilingual plaques, full-scale tactile replicas, and QR codes that, when scanned, instantly reveal the story of each space artifact. On the digital side, the platform runs through a Progressive Web App (PWA) and Augmented Reality (AR) application. Using official NASA data (such as JPL Horizons), the app functions as a pocket cosmic compass: users point their smartphones at the sky to track active missions or view the last recorded coordinates of probes, rovers, and landers that have lost contact with the agency, complemented by first-person logbooks and a gamified space passport.

What are its benefits?

The Katherine Johnson Space Heritage delivers significant educational and technological benefits by democratizing access to science—transforming complex technical data and closed NASA archives into intuitive educational content directly in streets and schools for students, teachers, and the general public. It fosters an engaging and inclusive learning experience by combining tactile, visual, and digital elements—such as augmented reality and full-scale replicas—that cater to diverse learning styles while ensuring accessibility through bilingual plaques and tactile reliefs. Furthermore, the platform removes technological barriers through a Progressive Web App (PWA) architecture accessible via QR code, eliminating the need for heavy native app downloads and operating smoothly even in areas with unstable internet connections (offline-first). Finally, conceived under a fully open-source model, the project ensures global scalability at low cost, allowing municipalities, universities, and institutions worldwide to manufacture totems locally and expand the network with minimal investment.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact of The Katherine Johnson Space Heritage spans educational, social, and technological fronts by actively inspiring new generations—with a special focus on students, minorities, and youth from underserved communities or public schools—to pursue paths in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), guided by the historic legacy of Katherine Johnson. It decentralizes scientific learning by moving it beyond traditional museums and turning plazas, sidewalks, and parks into vibrant, accessible public spaces for science outreach. Furthermore, the project preserves collective memory through "space archaeology," bringing visibility not only to major active missions but also to silent artifacts, inactive rovers, and lost probes across the vastness of the cosmos by sharing their stories of resilience and discovery. Ultimately, it aims to build a decentralized, collaborative global network of open-air museums made possible by an open-source model that allows any city or institution to replicate the totems and connect to the platform without financial or commercial barriers.

How is your project creative?

The creativity of The Katherine Johnson Space Heritage lies in the original way it approaches space exploration and reconnects it with people's everyday lives through an inversion of cosmic perspective: while most initiatives focus solely on rocket launches or future missions, this project brings visibility to "space archaeology"—rescuing the stories of inactive or lost rovers, landers, and probes resting silently across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. It creates an immersive fusion between the urban and the cosmic by transforming ordinary sidewalks, plazas, and parks into interactive extensions of global museums, bridging city concrete with the vastness of the universe through Augmented Reality (AR) without requiring complex or expensive physical structures. Furthermore, through gamification and narratives of presence, it converts abstract scientific data and cold NASA telemetry into immersive first-person logbooks and a digital space passport that users fill out as they interact with physical totems and uncover new celestial artifacts

What factors did your team consider?

The team considered several critical and strategic factors in developing The Katherine Johnson Space Heritage to ensure the solution would be viable, inclusive, and high-impact, starting with universal accessibility—guaranteeing physical and digital inclusion through bilingual plaques and full-scale tactile reliefs on the totems so that visually impaired individuals and people of all age groups can fully engage with the experience. Regarding economic feasibility and global scalability, the project was conceived under a fully open-source model, enabling municipalities, schools, and institutions worldwide to manufacture totems locally using accessible materials and join the network without financial barriers or prohibitive costs. In terms of technical resilience, the platform was engineered around an offline-first architecture tailored for public plazas, parks, and schoolyards that often suffer from unstable internet signals, leveraging Service Workers and local caching to ensure uninterrupted operation of the application and orbital ephemerides. Finally, the team prioritized ethical, privacy, and regulatory compliance by strictly adhering to the NASA hackathon's Terms and Conditions—relying exclusively on official public data without altering registered trademarks and refraining from collecting sensitive personal data from minors
